title: Diagnosing and Repairing Shape-Prior Shortcuts in Long-Range Single-Shot Fringe Projection Profilometry

paper.title: Diagnosing and Repairing Shape-Prior Shortcuts in Long-Range Single-Shot Fringe Projection Profilometry
paper.abstract: Abstract Learning-based single-shot fringe projection profilometry (FPP) has been studied primarily in the close-range regime (endoscopic, tabletop, and high-speed dynamic settings) where fringe contrast and triangulation geometry are favorable. The long-range regime (standoff beyond 1 m) remains largely unaddressed for three coupled reasons: the inverse-square falloff of light intensity reduces fringe signal-to-noise ratio and degrades the reliability of physical ground truth at these distances, the single-shot formulation is intrinsically ill-posed because fringe-order information is unavailable from one image, and the architectures used in this domain have not been studied mechanistically, leaving error diagnosis without principled guidance. We address these gaps in a unified diagnose-repair-verify study, with mechanistic interpretability (MI) and conformal uncertainty quantification (UQ) as the diagnostic instruments. Methodologically, MI and UQ are used as convergent diagnostics whose agreement on a single physical failure locus drives and then verifies an architectural repair, a diagnose-repair-verify template for physics-constrained learning that we apply here to long-range single-shot FPP. Systematic ablations on a photorealistic synthetic benchmark (15,600 fringe images, 50 objects at 1.5–2.1 m standoff) establish a best UNet baseline at 14.54 mm object mean absolute error (MAE). Three mechanistic probes (linear probing, Grad-CAM, in-range flat-plane out-of-distribution test) converge: the baseline solves the task via object-boundary shape priors rather than fringe-phase decoding. We repair this architecturally with PhiCalNet , whose operative design choice is to output a wrapped-phase representation rather than depth, with a fixed differentiable calibration layer mapping that phase to depth at the output. The shape-prior solution is therefore removed from the hypothesis space at the architectural level rather than discouraged via a loss penalty. A physics-informed loss baseline that enforces the same physics as a soft penalty on a depth-regressing network yields no measurable gain, isolating the architectural choice as the operative factor. PhiCalNet reduces object MAE 3.3 × \times to 4.46 mm; the residual is carried by 0.103% of pixels at the ± π \pm\pi wrap discontinuity, a structural limit of continuous regression of a discontinuous target. The same MI battery applied to PhiCalNet inverts the UNet profile, and pixel-wise conformal uncertainty quantification confirms the diagnosis from the outside: rejecting the top 5% of object pixels by snapshot disagreement reduces PhiCalNet root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 64% (20.6 → \rightarrow 7.4 mm) versus 3.5% for the baseline. MI and UQ converge on the same failure locus.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Fringe projection profilometry (FPP) is a non-contact dense 3D measurement technique capable of achieving sub-millimeter accuracy. As a result, it has seen widespread use across domains where high-precision metrology is demanded, including surface inspection ( Qian et al., 2021 ; Deng et al., 2016 ) , robotic scanning ( Haroon et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ) , and manufacturing process control ( Zhang et al., 2023a ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) . A key component of this accuracy is multi-step phase-shifting acquisition ( Zhang, 2016 ; Geng, 2011 ) , in which multiple phase-shifted fringe patterns are projected and analytically combined to recover depth. While this multi-step capture is responsible for the technique’s measurement fidelity, it also requires the scene, the camera-projector geometry, and the illumination to remain stable across the full sequence, restricting traditional FPP to controlled tabletop setups. Recent advances in machine and deep learning have therefore motivated single-shot reconstruction, in which depth is recovered from one fringe image rather than from a phase-shifted sequence ( Zuo et al., 2022 ; Van der Jeught and Dirckx, 2019 ; Nguyen et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Ikeda et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Balasubramaniam and Li, 2023 ; Wang and Xing, 2025 ) , lifting this constraint and enabling real-time measurement under non-stationary conditions such as moving objects, perturbed sensor positions, or variable lighting. The active deep-learning single-shot literature has nevertheless concentrated almost exclusively on the short-range regime below 1 m standoff, with endoscopic ( Zuo et al., 2025 ) and tabletop ( Wang et al., 2021 ) setups being typical. To extend FPP beyond controlled lab settings to real-world deployments where non-stationarity is inherent, such as inspecting objects too large to bring to a scanner, scanning scenes that require wider fields of view, or measuring targets the sensor cannot physically approach, long-range capability becomes necessary.

sections.heading: Yet long range is the harder regime, by orders of magnitude.
sections.text: The close-range regime in which current methods operate spans a narrow range of geometries: endoscopic and microscopic systems below 100 mm standoff, tabletop systems at 300–800 mm, and high-speed dynamic measurements that exploit the same close-range geometry to track motion. Wang et al.’s graphics-augmented SSSR-FPP ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , Nguyen et al.’s structured-light DCNN ( Nguyen et al., 2020 ) , Van der Jeught and Dirckx’s single-shot SLP ( Van der Jeught and Dirckx, 2019 ) , Ikeda et al.’s color-fringe approach ( Ikeda et al., 2025 ) , Li et al.’s inner-shifting-phase encoding ( Li et al., 2025 ) , Zhu et al.’s Hformer ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) , and Balasubramaniam and Li’s data-storage measurement ( Balasubramaniam and Li, 2023 ) all target this close-range regime. At long range the physics is qualitatively different. Structured-light signal-to-noise ratio degrades as 1 / r 2 1/r^{2} , fringe contrast drops as the projected pattern spreads, and depth resolution at fixed baseline degrades quadratically with range. This property of light makes it difficult to obtain a solid ground truth. The same physics also produces a fringe-order ambiguity whose induced depth error scales as Z 2 Z^{2} in the working distance; Section 4.2 formalizes both consequences and pinpoints why the single-shot fringe-to-depth mapping is more severely ill-posed at long range than at close range.

sections.heading: Ground truth at long range is itself unsolved.
sections.text: Acquiring accurate physical ground truth at standoff > 1 >1 m is hard for reasons independent of any learning method. Reference measurements at these distances typically require coordinate-measuring machines or terrestrial laser scanners with their own millimeter-scale uncertainties, and registering those measurements to the camera frame with sub-millimeter accuracy is nontrivial. The regime is data-starved as a direct consequence. A validated synthetic pipeline sidesteps this. VIRTUS-FPP ( Haroon et al., 2026 ) demonstrates a photorealistic virtual FPP framework in NVIDIA Isaac Sim whose fringe contrast, phase-unwrapping behavior, and depth-reconstruction accuracy are validated against physical measurements; building the benchmark on this validated framework makes long-range ground truth tractable at the scale ML training requires. The novelty of the regime and the difficulty of physical ground truth are therefore coupled: the simulator is the methodological move that makes the regime accessible at all.

sections.heading: No shared benchmark or evaluation convention.
sections.text: Beyond the long-range gap, single-shot ML FPP as a whole lacks the shared infrastructure that mainstream computer vision takes for granted ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Lin et al., 2014 ) . Across the literature, normalization conventions ( Feng et al., 2021 ; Ikeda et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2020 ) , loss functions ( Wang and Xing, 2025 ; Ikeda et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ) , evaluation regions, and aggregate metrics all vary, and cross-study comparison is therefore unreliable. Prior synthetic-data efforts ( Zheng et al., 2020 ; Ueda et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2023b ) demonstrate photorealistic FPP simulation but do not release the resulting datasets, limiting their utility as shared benchmarks. The recent single-shot structured-light benchmark of Evans et al. ( Evans et al., 2024 ) provides an open real-data dataset, but on a calibration target with random surface variations rather than object-diverse self-occluding geometries. As a result, no open-source photorealistic synthetic benchmark for single-shot FPP is currently available, and none of the existing datasets cover object-diverse self-occluding geometries at long-range standoff. Explicit reporting conventions for normalization, loss, masking, and training-set composition are similarly absent.

sections.heading: The interpretive gap.
sections.text: Within the single-shot literature, methods are trained end-to-end with pixelwise regression and evaluated only on aggregate reconstruction error ( Zuo et al., 2022 ; Ikeda et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . This leaves open whether they recover depth from the phase structure of the fringe pattern or from object-level shape cues that happen to correlate with depth in the training distribution. This is the shortcut-learning hypothesis of Geirhos et al. ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) , and in metrology it has direct consequences: a shape-prior network will not generalize to novel geometries and cannot substitute for phase-based reconstruction even when aggregate error looks competitive. The residual error single-shot networks hit at long range may reflect this representational issue rather than capacity or data scarcity, but the question has not been adjudicated mechanistically.

sections.heading: This paper.
sections.text: We address these gaps in a unified diagnose-repair-verify study, with mechanistic interpretability (MI) and conformal uncertainty quantification (UQ) as the diagnostic instruments throughout. FPP-ML-Bench ( S. et al., 2026 ) is built on the VIRTUS-FPP framework: 15,600 fringe images, 300 depth reconstructions, 50 objects at 1.5–2.1 m standoff, with a standardized object/background/overall evaluation protocol we show can change reported object-only error by nearly an order of magnitude. Systematic ablations on this benchmark isolate the design choices that govern single-shot FPP performance: individual depth normalization improves object MAE 9.1 × \times over raw depth; removing background fringes degrades performance 2.8–7.3 × \times (background fringes are signal, not noise); homogeneous multi-frame training with phase-shifted frames of a single orientation improves object MAE by 20–24% while mixing orientations degrades performance; Hybrid L1 ( α = 0.7 \alpha\!=\!0.7 ) is optimal; UNet outperforms TransUNet by 29%, ResUNet by 60%, and Pix2Pix by 91%. The 1.9 × \times spread across architectures and the 14.54 mm residual (18% of the 80 mm object depth range) point to a representational rather than a model-capacity limit. Three mechanistic probes (linear probing, Grad-CAM, and an in-range flat-plane out-of-distribution test), to our knowledge the first application of mechanistic interpretability to FPP, converge on the diagnosis: the best UNet baseline solves the task via object-boundary shape priors rather than via the phase structure of the fringe pattern. Additional data or larger models will not close the gap because they do not change the hypothesis space the optimizer searches. We repair this architecturally with PhiCalNet . The operative design choice is not the calibration math itself (every phase-intermediate FPP network has classical triangulation calibration sitting somewhere in the pipeline) but a specific architectural framing: the network’s output is wrapped phase ( sin ⁡ ϕ , cos ⁡ ϕ ) (\sin\phi,\cos\phi) rather than depth, and the only path from that output to the reconstructed depth runs through a fixed differentiable calibration layer that applies the FPP triangulation physics deterministically. The shape-prior solution available to a depth-regressing network is therefore removed from the hypothesis space architecturally rather than discouraged via a loss penalty, because the network never produces depth as a direct learned quantity. A physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline that enforces the same physics as a soft loss penalty on an otherwise unconstrained depth-regressing network yields no measurable gain across a λ \lambda sweep, isolating the architectural-versus-loss-level choice as the operative factor. PhiCalNet reduces single-shot object MAE by 3.3 × \times over the UNet baseline (4.46 vs. 14.54 mm); a three-frame extension reduces this further to 1.16 mm, and a fringe-order sensitivity sweep shows the oracle- k k assumption is a convenient formalism rather than a strict deployment requirement. Beyond the headline single-shot phase-only configuration reported here, the differentiability of the calibration layer activates a depth-supervised gradient path that runs from the depth output back through the calibration and into the learnable backbone, opening a family of natural joint-learning extensions of the design (joint calibration learning, heteroscedastic depth likelihoods, multi-resolution depth losses, absolute-scale depth supervision) that we sketch in the conclusion. We verify the repair from two independent angles. The same MI battery applied to PhiCalNet inverts the UNet profile: phase becomes the most decodable internal feature (depth has no explicit internal representation, consistent with the calibration layer carrying the geometric transform), a dual-mode Grad-CAM analysis on the same trained weights shows fringe-favored attention at the layers driving the phase output with edge bias appearing only when gradients flow through the calibration layer, and the flat-plane test recovers a coherent ( sin ⁡ ϕ , cos ⁡ ϕ ) (\sin\phi,\cos\phi) field with the correct quadrature offset. Pixel-wise conformal uncertainty quantification using a snapshot ensemble (to our knowledge the first application of conformal prediction to FPP, and one of the first to pixel-wise depth regression more broadly ( Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023 ) ) confirms the diagnosis from the outside: rejecting the top 5% of object pixels by snapshot standard deviation reduces PhiCalNet RMSE by 64% (20.6 → \rightarrow 7.4 mm) while reducing the UNet baseline’s RMSE by only 3.5% (28.4 → \rightarrow 27.4 mm). MI and UQ converge on the same failure population. FPP makes this convergence test substantially more diagnostic than the diffuse linguistic or medical settings where joint MI and UQ analysis has prior precedent: the network’s failure modes have a single physical locus (the ± π \pm\pi wrap discontinuity), and MI inspection of internals, the residual-error spatial structure, and UQ inspection of self-reported confidence can be compared at that single locus and shown to agree. We treat this three-way convergence as a methodological contribution beyond the FPP-specific result.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: This paper makes the following contributions. We adopt FPP-ML-Bench ( S. et al., 2026 ) , the first open-source photorealistic synthetic benchmark for single-shot FPP, which covers object-diverse self-occluding geometries at long-range standoff (1.5–2.1 m) with a standardized object/background/overall evaluation protocol and explicit reporting conventions for normalization, loss, masking, and training-set composition. We isolate the design choices that govern single-shot FPP performance through systematic ablations of normalization, background processing, multi-frame composition, loss design, and architecture, and find that the residual error of the best baseline reflects a representational rather than a capacity-bound limit. We diagnose that representational limit via the first application of mechanistic interpretability to FPP, with three complementary probes (linear probing, Grad-CAM, and an in-range flat-plane out-of-distribution test) converging on the finding that the best UNet baseline solves the task via shape priors rather than fringe-phase decoding. We introduce PhiCalNet, a phase-intermediate architecture whose operative design choice is a phase-only output space coupled with a fixed differentiable calibration layer that maps phase to depth deterministically, and demonstrate via a PINN counterfactual that the architectural framing rather than the physics-in-the-loss is the operative factor. We characterize the residual wrap-boundary error of PhiCalNet analytically and empirically, and show that a multi-frame extension closes the gap as the information-theoretic argument predicts. We verify the repair via the same MI battery applied to PhiCalNet, which inverts the UNet profile across all three probes, and via the first application of conformal prediction to FPP, with a dual-mode Grad-CAM analysis that isolates the calibration layer as the source of depth-output edge bias. The MI and UQ convergence at a single geometric locus is offered as a methodological template applicable to other physics-informed learning settings.

sections.heading: Paper organization.
sections.text: Section 2 reviews the FPP pipeline and describes the VIRTUS-FPP framework used for data acquisition. Section 3 describes the dataset and acquisition protocol. The benchmarking section that follows formalizes the single-shot setting and its theoretical limits (Section 4.2 ) and establishes the single-shot baseline through systematic ablations of normalization (Section 4.3 ), background processing (Section 4.3.4 ), multi-frame composition (Section 4.4 ), loss design (Section 4.5 ), and architecture (Section 4.6 ). Section 4.7 runs the mechanistic diagnosis on the best baseline. Section 5 introduces PhiCalNet and the PINN contrast, with the multi-frame and sensitivity studies in Section 5.6 . Section 5.7 verifies the repair mechanistically, and Section 5.8 verifies it via uncertainty quantification. Section 6 concludes.

sections.heading: 2 Fringe Projection Profilometry
sections.text: This section reviews the classical FPP pipeline on which the rest of the paper builds (Section 2.1 ) and describes the virtual implementation used for data acquisition (Sections 2.2 – 2.3 ). The virtual implementation is based on the VIRTUS-FPP ( Haroon et al., 2026 ) framework.

sections.heading: 2.1 Principles
sections.text: FPP recovers per-pixel depth by projecting structured fringe patterns onto a scene and decoding the phase modulation that surface geometry imposes on those patterns ( Zhang, 2016 ; Geng, 2011 ) . The classical pipeline decomposes into three deterministic stages: wrapped phase recovery, fringe-order recovery, and triangulation.

Acquiring the full N N -step sequence and demodulating analytically gives the wrapped phase ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) = − tan − 1 ⁡ ( ∑ n = 1 N I n sin δ n ∑ n = 1 N I n cos δ n ) . \phi(x,y)=-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N}I_{n}\sin\delta_{n}}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}I_{n}\cos\delta_{n}}\right). (2) N N typically ranges from 4 for fast acquisition to 18 for high noise immunity ( Zhang, 2016 ) .

sections.heading: Fringe-order recovery.
sections.text: The wrapped phase ϕ \phi is ambiguous modulo 2 ​ π 2\pi across multiple fringe periods. The absolute phase Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) = ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) + 2 ​ π ​ k ​ ( x , y ) \Phi(x,y)=\phi(x,y)+2\pi k(x,y) (3) requires the integer fringe order k ⁡ ( x , y ) ∈ ℤ k(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z} at every pixel. Classical FPP recovers k k by an auxiliary procedure such as temporal unwrapping with gray-code projection, in which a separate set of binary patterns is projected alongside the fringe sequence and decoded into the fringe index at every pixel ( Sansoni et al., 1999 ) .

sections.heading: Triangulation.
sections.text: With calibrated camera and projector pinhole models M c M^{c} and M p M^{p} , the absolute phase at each camera pixel maps to a projector coordinate via u p = Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ T p / ( 2 ​ π ) u^{p}=\Phi(x,y)\,T_{p}/(2\pi) , where T p T_{p} is the projector pixel period. The 3D point is recovered by triangulating the camera ray (from the camera pixel) and the projector ray (from the recovered projector coordinate) ( Zhang, 2010 ) . Classical FPP achieves sub-millimeter accuracy because every stage of the pipeline is deterministic and well-posed: the N N -step capture uniquely determines ϕ \phi , gray-code decoding uniquely determines k k , and calibrated triangulation maps Φ \Phi to depth. The single-shot setting that motivates this paper replaces both analytical stages with a single learned mapping from one fringe image to depth; Section 4.2 formalizes the ambiguity that this collapse introduces. Training and evaluating such a mapping at long range requires paired fringe-depth data at a scale physical acquisition cannot reliably provide, for the reasons given in Section 1 ; we therefore instantiate the classical pipeline above in a calibrated virtual FPP system, the VIRTUS-FPP framework ( Haroon et al., 2026 ) , and the remainder of this section describes its configuration and calibration.

sections.heading: 2.2 System Configuration
sections.text: VIRTUS-FPP is built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, integrating OptiX ray tracing for photorealistic rendering, PhysX for physics, and Universal Scene Description (USD) for 3D composition. The virtual system consists of a calibrated camera-projector pair (Table 1 ). The camera uses Isaac Sim’s pinhole primitive ( 960 × 960 960\times 960 resolution, 50 cm focal length), while the projector is modeled using a rectangular light source ( 0.625 ​ m × 0.5 ​ m 0.625\text{ m}\times 0.5\text{ m} , 40 nits) with texture projection. This physics-based approach captures complex light transport including multi-bounce illumination, surface reflectivity variations, and ambient occlusion.

sections.text: VIRTUS-FPP performs complete virtual calibration using procedurally generated 5 × 9 5\times 9 asymmetric circular boards (10 mm diameter, 20 mm spacing). The system captures 18 calibration poses yielding 936 calibration images in approximately 5 minutes (10,530 images/hour). The calibrated system achieves sub-pixel accuracy (stereo reprojection error: 0.055506 pixels, projector error: 0.048609 pixels). ( Haroon et al., 2026 ) The VIRTUS-FPP simulation setup is illustrated in Fig. 1 . sections.heading: 3.1 Dataset Composition
sections.text: We collected data for 50 USD objects from the YCB dataset ( Calli et al., 2017 ) and NVIDIA Physical AI Warehouse ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) spanning cylindrical containers, rectangular boxes, complex shapes (power drills, spray guns), and industrial components. This diversity evaluates robustness across varying surface characteristics and morphological complexity, from simple geometric primitives to intricate shapes with concavities and fine-scale features. The system was calibrated and operated within a range of 1.5–2.1 m, with all objects positioned and scanned at distances within this range. Objects were placed on a background plane with identical matte properties to provide consistent lighting conditions and minimize unwanted reflections. For multi-view acquisition, each object was rotated about the vertical axis in 60 ∘ 60^{\circ} increments using the rotation matrix: R z ​ ( θ i ) = [ cos ⁡ θ i − sin ⁡ θ i 0 sin ⁡ θ i cos ⁡ θ i 0 0 0 1 ] R_{z}(\theta_{i})=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta_{i}&-\sin\theta_{i}&0\\ \sin\theta_{i}&\cos\theta_{i}&0\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix} (5) for θ i = i ⋅ 60 ∘ \theta_{i}=i\cdot 60^{\circ} where i = 0 , 1 , … , 5 i=0,1,\ldots,5 . This yields 6 viewpoints per object with approximately 50% overlap between adjacent views.

sections.heading: 3.3 Dataset Summary
sections.text: The dataset comprises 15,600 raw fringe images (50 objects × \times 6 viewpoints × \times 52 fringe patterns per sequence), 300 corresponding ground truth depth maps stored as .mat files, and 50 ground truth mesh geometries. Data are partitioned with an 80/10/10 split at the object level: 240 training samples (40 objects × \times 6 viewpoints), 30 validation samples (5 objects × \times 6 viewpoints), and 30 test samples (5 objects × \times 6 viewpoints), ensuring evaluation on completely unseen object geometries. sections.heading: 4.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: The classical FPP pipeline reviewed in Section 2.1 acquires N N phase-shifted fringe images to recover the wrapped phase analytically and a separate gray-code sequence to recover the integer fringe order, then triangulates to depth. Single-shot reconstruction collapses this pipeline to a single fringe image I I and replaces both analytical stages with a learned mapping D ^ norm = f θ ​ ( I ) \hat{D}_{\mathrm{norm}}=f_{\theta}(I) , where f θ f_{\theta} is a neural network. We use the first fringe from each 18-step sequence as input, ensuring identical conditions across models. This collapsed formulation is inherently ill-posed. Single fringe images contain ambiguity in depth estimation owing to the periodic nature of sinusoidal patterns: in the absence of phase-shifting redundancy or auxiliary unwrapping patterns, each 2 ​ π 2\pi phase range looks identical to every other, and the fringe-order ambiguity that classical gray-code decoding resolves analytically is no longer separable from phase prediction. As a result, learning-based approaches rely on inferring depth from learned shape priors and statistical regularities rather than from fully explicit geometric cues alone. Section 4.2 formalizes this ambiguity and shows that the depth error induced by an incorrect fringe-order estimate scales quadratically with the working distance, accounting on theoretical grounds for why single-shot FPP is particularly difficult at long range. We ablate the five design choices that govern single-shot FPP performance: depth normalization, background processing, multi-frame composition, loss function, and architecture. This isolates the impact of each and establishes best practices for learning-based single-shot FPP.

sections.heading: 4.2 Theoretical Analysis: Single-Shot Ambiguity and Long-Range Sensitivity
sections.text: We formalize the ambiguity induced by using a single fringe image for depth reconstruction. Consider a projector-camera system in which a sinusoidal fringe pattern is projected onto a scene and observed by the camera. The captured image intensity at camera pixel ( x , y ) (x,y) for the t t -th phase-shifted pattern can be modeled as I t ​ ( x , y ) = A ⁡ ( x , y ) + B ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ cos ⁡ ( Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) + δ t ) , I_{t}(x,y)=A(x,y)+B(x,y)\cos\!\left(\Phi(x,y)+\delta_{t}\right), (9) where A ⁡ ( x , y ) A(x,y) is the background illumination, B ⁡ ( x , y ) B(x,y) is the fringe modulation, δ t \delta_{t} is the known phase shift, and Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) \Phi(x,y) is the absolute phase associated with the projector-camera correspondence. The absolute phase decomposes as Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) = ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) + 2 ​ π ​ k ​ ( x , y ) , \Phi(x,y)=\phi(x,y)+2\pi k(x,y), (10) where ϕ ( x , y ) ∈ [ − π , π ) \phi(x,y)\in[-\pi,\pi) is the wrapped phase and k ⁡ ( x , y ) ∈ ℤ k(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z} is the fringe order. The wrapped phase describes the local phase within one fringe period, whereas the fringe order identifies the global fringe period to which the observed point belongs. Proposition 1 . In single-shot sinusoidal fringe projection profilometry, the mapping from a single captured fringe image I t ​ ( x , y ) I_{t}(x,y) to scene depth Z ⁡ ( x , y ) Z(x,y) is not uniquely determined unless the fringe order k ⁡ ( x , y ) k(x,y) is known or otherwise constrained. Proof. From Eq. ( 9 ), the observed intensity depends on the absolute phase through a cosine function. Since the cosine function is periodic with period 2 ​ π 2\pi , for any integer m ∈ ℤ m\in\mathbb{Z} , cos ⁡ ( Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) + δ t ) = cos ⁡ ( Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) + 2 ​ π ​ m + δ t ) . \cos\!\left(\Phi(x,y)+\delta_{t}\right)=\cos\!\left(\Phi(x,y)+2\pi m+\delta_{t}\right). (11) Therefore, two absolute phases Φ 1 ​ ( x , y ) = ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) + 2 ​ π ​ k ​ ( x , y ) \Phi_{1}(x,y)=\phi(x,y)+2\pi k(x,y) (12) and Φ 2 ​ ( x , y ) = ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) + 2 ​ π ​ ( k ⁡ ( x , y ) + m ) , m ≠ 0 , \Phi_{2}(x,y)=\phi(x,y)+2\pi\left(k(x,y)+m\right),\qquad m\neq 0, (13) produce identical observed intensities: I t ​ ( Φ 1 ​ ( x , y ) ) = I t ​ ( Φ 2 ​ ( x , y ) ) . I_{t}\!\left(\Phi_{1}(x,y)\right)=I_{t}\!\left(\Phi_{2}(x,y)\right). (14) However, these two absolute phases correspond to different projector coordinates. If the projected fringe pitch is P P pixels, the projector coordinate associated with the absolute phase is u p ​ ( x , y ) = P 2 ​ π ​ Φ ​ ( x , y ) . u_{p}(x,y)=\frac{P}{2\pi}\,\Phi(x,y). (15) Substituting Eq. ( 10 ) into Eq. ( 15 ) gives u p ​ ( x , y ) = P ⁡ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) 2 ​ π + k ⁡ ( x , y ) ) . u_{p}(x,y)=P\!\left(\frac{\phi(x,y)}{2\pi}+k(x,y)\right). (16) Thus, changing the fringe order by m m changes the projector coordinate by Δ ​ u p = m ​ P . \Delta u_{p}=mP. (17) Although the observed intensity is unchanged under this shift, the projector-camera correspondence is not. Since depth reconstruction in FPP is obtained through triangulation from the camera pixel and the corresponding projector coordinate, different values of u p u_{p} generally yield different depths. The same single-shot intensity observation is therefore consistent with multiple physically distinct depths. Hence, the mapping I t ​ ( x , y ) ↦ Z ⁡ ( x , y ) I_{t}(x,y)\mapsto Z(x,y) (18) is non-injective in the absence of fringe-order information. ∎

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Effect of Range on Depth Error
sections.text: We next show that an incorrect fringe-order estimate produces increasingly large depth errors as the object distance increases. For clarity, consider a simplified triangulation model analogous to stereo geometry: Z = f ​ b d , Z=\frac{fb}{d}, (19) where Z Z is depth, f f is the focal length, b b is the projector-camera baseline, and d d is the disparity induced by the projector-camera correspondence. A perturbation in correspondence produces a depth perturbation Δ ​ Z ≈ ∂ Z ∂ d ​ Δ ​ d . \Delta Z\approx\frac{\partial Z}{\partial d}\,\Delta d. (20) Differentiating Eq. ( 19 ) with respect to d d gives ∂ Z ∂ d = − f ​ b d 2 . \frac{\partial Z}{\partial d}=-\frac{fb}{d^{2}}. (21) Since d = f ​ b / Z d=fb/Z , Eq. ( 21 ) can be rewritten as | Δ ​ Z | ≈ Z 2 f ​ b ​ | Δ ​ d | . \left|\Delta Z\right|\approx\frac{Z^{2}}{fb}\left|\Delta d\right|. (22) A fringe-order error of m m periods induces a projector-coordinate error of approximately m ​ P mP and therefore a correspondence error proportional to m ​ P mP : | Δ ​ Z | ∝ Z 2 f ​ b ​ | m ​ P | . \left|\Delta Z\right|\propto\frac{Z^{2}}{fb}\,|mP|. (23) Equation ( 23 ) shows that the depth error caused by an incorrect fringe order grows approximately quadratically with the object distance Z Z . While fringe-order ambiguity exists at all working distances, its effect becomes significantly more severe in long-range FPP, explaining why single-shot fringe-to-depth learning becomes increasingly ill-posed at distances greater than approximately one meter, where a small correspondence ambiguity can lead to a large depth error. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis to characterize how fringe-order ambiguity governs depth error specifically in the long-range single-shot FPP regime, which the existing single-shot literature has not addressed.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Implication for Learning-Based Single-Shot FPP
sections.text: The above result has a direct implication for learning-based single-shot FPP. If a neural network is trained to directly learn f θ : I t ​ ( x , y ) ↦ Z ⁡ ( x , y ) , f_{\theta}:I_{t}(x,y)\mapsto Z(x,y), (24) then it is asked to approximate a mapping that may not be uniquely defined. In particular, two points may have identical or nearly identical local fringe observations, I t ( 1 ) ​ ( x , y ) ≈ I t ( 2 ) ​ ( x , y ) , I_{t}^{(1)}(x,y)\approx I_{t}^{(2)}(x,y), (25) while corresponding to different depths, Z ( 1 ) ​ ( x , y ) ≠ Z ( 2 ) ​ ( x , y ) , Z^{(1)}(x,y)\neq Z^{(2)}(x,y), (26) because they belong to different fringe orders. Under standard regression losses such as ℓ 1 \ell_{1} or ℓ 2 \ell_{2} loss, the network may learn an averaged or biased depth estimate rather than the physically correct depth. The implication is that, for long-range single-shot FPP, the network must be provided with additional information that resolves the phase ambiguity. This can take several forms: explicit supervision of the fringe order k ⁡ ( x , y ) k(x,y) , recovery of the absolute phase Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) \Phi(x,y) , spatial or temporal coding constraints, or an auxiliary phase-unwrapping objective. In any of these formulations, the reconstruction pipeline becomes I t ​ ( x , y ) ↦ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x , y ) , k ⁡ ( x , y ) ) ↦ Φ ⁡ ( x , y ) ↦ Z ⁡ ( x , y ) , I_{t}(x,y)\mapsto\left(\phi(x,y),k(x,y)\right)\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\mapsto Z(x,y), (27) rather than directly learning an ill-posed mapping from a single fringe image to depth. PhiCalNet (Section 5 ) is one realization of this pipeline. The empirical predictions of this analysis are confirmed in the remainder of the paper. The architectural baselines of Section 4.6 all plateau in the regime that Proposition 1 predicts is irreducibly ill-posed without fringe-order information, with errors that the mechanistic analysis of Section 4.7 traces directly to the network’s inability to recover phase. The residual-error analysis of PhiCalNet in Section 5.5 localizes the model’s residual to the ± π \pm\pi wrap-boundary pixels identified above as the locus of the underlying ambiguity, with the catastrophic-error magnitude observed there matching the one fringe period × Z 2 / ( f ​ b ) \times Z^{2}/(fb) scaling of Eq. ( 23 ).

sections.heading: 4.3 Normalization Strategy Comparison
sections.text: Having formalized the limit set by single-shot fringe-order ambiguity, we now turn to the empirical question of how well a learning-based mapping can be made to perform within that limit. We begin by isolating data normalization, which we will see is the single most impactful design choice for an end-to-end depth-regression baseline; the remaining subsections then sweep background processing, multi-frame composition, loss design, and architecture in turn.

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Architecture and training configuration
sections.text: We use UNet ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) as our baseline architecture due to its widespread adoption in FPP literature ( Feng et al., 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2020 ; Ikeda et al., 2025 ) and strong performance on dense prediction tasks. The network consists of four encoder-decoder stages, progressively downsampling from 960 × 960 960\times 960 to 60 × 60 60\times 60 resolution, with channel depths increasing from 64 to 1024 at the bottleneck. Each encoder and decoder stage uses two 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions followed by instance normalization and ReLU activation. Skip connections preserve spatial information across corresponding encoder-decoder levels. We train with RMSE loss using the RMSprop optimizer ( α = 0.99 \alpha=0.99 , initial learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} ), batch size 4, and a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler (factor=0.5, patience=10 epochs, minimum learning rate 10 − 6 10^{-6} ). This combination has demonstrated effectiveness for similar dense regression tasks ( Ikeda et al., 2025 ) and provides a stable baseline for comparison. Training continues until the learning rate reaches its minimum threshold, indicating convergence.

(29) • Object error: Computed only on pixels where ground truth depth is non-zero ( D ⁡ ( u , v ) > 0 D(u,v)>0 for raw/global normalizations, or D norm ​ ( u , v ) > 0 D_{\mathrm{norm}}(u,v)>0 for individual normalization), isolating prediction accuracy on the actual object geometry. Natural phase discontinuities at object boundaries provide clearer edge information than the artificial black-to-object transitions created by masking, allowing the network to learn where fringe patterns abruptly change phase as indicators of depth transitions. Additionally, background pixels provide training signal and implicit regularization, helping the network understand the overall fringe-to-depth relationship and preventing overfitting to object-only patterns. This finding has important implications for FPP learning: background fringes are signal , not noise. All subsequent experiments therefore use full fringe patterns with background intact.

sections.heading: 4.4 Multi-Frame Training Ablation
sections.text: Having established individual normalization and background retention as optimal, we investigate whether expanding the training set using additional fringe frames from each acquisition sequence improves reconstruction accuracy. In FPP-ML-Bench, each object-viewpoint combination yields 52 captured images: 18 horizontal sinusoidal fringe patterns (varying phase), 18 vertical sinusoidal fringe patterns, 7 horizontal gray code patterns, 7 vertical gray code patterns, one black image, and one white image. All 52 images share the same ground truth depth map. The baseline experiments above use only the first horizontal fringe image (frame 0) as input, yielding 240 training samples. Here, we evaluate whether pairing additional frames with the same depth targets, effectively treating each frame as an independent training sample, improves generalization.

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: We train the same UNet architecture with identical hyperparameters under four multi-frame conditions: 1. Horizontal only: 18 horizontal sinusoidal frames per sequence (4,320 training / 540 test samples). 2. Vertical only: 18 vertical sinusoidal frames per sequence (4,320 training / 540 test samples). 3. All sinusoidal: All 36 sinusoidal frames (horizontal + vertical) per sequence (8,640 training / 1,080 test samples). 4. All frames: All 52 frames including gray code, black, and white patterns (12,480 training / 1,560 test samples). Each condition is evaluated on its corresponding test set, where each test sample pairs a fringe frame with the same ground truth depth map used in the baseline.

Training on all 18 phase-shifted frames from a single fringe orientation yields the largest improvements. Horizontal-only training reduces object MAE by 20.6% (16.20 mm to 12.87 mm), while vertical-only training achieves a 23.7% reduction (16.20 mm to 12.36 mm). Both single-orientation conditions also dramatically improve background suppression, reducing background MAE by 77–83% (0.92 mm to 0.16–0.21 mm). The improvement in background prediction is expected: with 18 different phase patterns projected onto the background during training, the network learns that varying fringe intensity on background regions should always map to zero depth, regardless of phase. This diversity forces the model to distinguish “fringe pattern on object” (which carries depth information) from “fringe pattern on background” (which should be suppressed). We note that the multi-frame conditions are evaluated over larger test sets (540–1,560 samples) than the baseline (30 samples), which reduces per-sample variance and yields more statistically reliable estimates. The tighter error distributions visible in Figs. 7 – 8 compared to the baseline (Fig. 3 ) partly reflect this difference in sample size. Combining horizontal and vertical orientations (all sinusoidal, 8,640 samples) performs worse than either orientation alone despite having 2 × 2\times more training data. Object MAE increases to 15.33 mm, only marginally better than the 240-sample baseline. Including all 52 frames further degrades object accuracy to 20.32 mm, worse than the baseline. This suggests that the UNet struggles to learn a single mapping that generalizes across fundamentally different fringe orientations. Horizontal and vertical fringes encode depth information along orthogonal axes, producing qualitatively different intensity patterns for the same geometry. Rather than benefiting from this diversity, the network appears to compromise between conflicting input-output relationships, diluting the learned representation. These results demonstrate that multi-frame training is beneficial only when the additional frames are homogeneous in orientation. Phase diversity within a single orientation acts as effective data augmentation, teaching the network phase-invariant depth extraction. However, orientation diversity introduces conflicting gradients that degrade performance. This finding has practical implications: when expanding FPP training datasets, practitioners should prefer additional phase-shifted frames from the same projection orientation rather than mixing orientations or including structurally different patterns such as gray code. For the remaining experiments in this paper, we continue using the single-frame baseline dataset (240 training samples) to isolate the effects of loss function and architecture choices independently of dataset size. Although vertical-only training achieves the lowest absolute error, the subsequent comparisons evaluate relative performance between configurations rather than absolute accuracy, and the conclusions regarding loss function ranking and architectural ordering are expected to generalize across training data compositions.

sections.heading: 4.7 Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
sections.text: The previous sections established that even the best-performing model (UNet with Hybrid L1 loss) achieves only 14.54 mm object MAE, representing 18% of the object depth range. To understand why this performance gap exists, we employ mechanistic interpretability, a set of techniques from machine learning research that aim to understand how neural networks arrive at their predictions by examining their internal representations and computational mechanisms. ( Olah et al., 2020 ) To our knowledge, this is the first application of mechanistic interpretability to FPP. Unlike standard evaluation metrics that only assess prediction accuracy, mechanistic interpretability provides insight into the features and strategies a network has learned. This distinction is critical: a network may achieve reasonable accuracy through shortcuts or heuristics that differ fundamentally from the intended solution. In our context, a network trained to predict depth from fringe patterns could potentially learn two very different strategies: (1) physics-based decoding , where the network extracts phase information from fringe intensity variations and converts it to depth following the mathematical relationship governing FPP; or (2) geometric shortcut learning , where the network recognizes object shapes from the training data and predicts depth by filling in learned shape templates, bypassing the fringe pattern entirely. We hypothesize that our networks learn the geometric shortcut rather than the physics-based solution. To test this, we employ three complementary interpretability techniques: linear probing to examine what information is encoded in intermediate representations, gradient-weighted class activation mapping (GradCAM) to visualize spatial attention patterns, and out-of-distribution testing with a featureless flat plane to expose reliance on geometric cues.

sections.heading: 4.7.1 Linear Probing Analysis
sections.text: Linear probing is a widely-used interpretability technique that determines what information is accessible in a network’s internal representations. ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ) The approach trains small auxiliary “probe” networks to predict specific target quantities from frozen intermediate activations. If a probe can accurately predict a target, that information must be explicitly encoded (or easily computable from) the activations; if the probe fails, the information is either absent or encoded in a form that is difficult to extract. Crucially, linear probing reveals what information the network represents , not merely what it receives as input. A network processing fringe images necessarily receives intensity patterns as input, but this does not mean those patterns are preserved or utilized in deeper layers. By probing intermediate activations, we can determine whether the network maintains fringe pattern information for depth computation or discards it in favor of geometric features. We train spatial probes to predict two types of targets from UNet activations: (1) geometric features (edge maps computed via Sobel filtering of the ground truth depth), representing structural boundary information; and (2) depth values , representing the physical quantity the network should predict. For each of the nine UNet layers (four encoder, bottleneck, four decoder), we train a probe network consisting of four convolutional layers to predict either edges or depth from frozen activations. Probe performance is measured by validation MSE loss, where lower loss indicates the target is more easily decoded from the activations. Table 7 and Fig. 15 show that geometric features (edges) are consistently easier to decode than depth values across all layers. The average probe loss for edges (0.000379) is 2.82 × \times lower than for depth (0.001069), indicating that the network’s internal representations encode geometric structure more explicitly than depth values. This asymmetry is particularly pronounced in decoder layers (dec3, dec4), where edge information is most accessible, precisely where the network should be refining depth predictions. sections.heading: 4.7.2 GradCAM Attention Analysis
sections.text: While linear probing reveals what information is encoded in network activations, it does not directly show what information the network uses for prediction. To address this, we employ Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (GradCAM), ( Selvaraju et al., 2017 ) a technique that visualizes which spatial regions of the input most strongly influence the network’s output. GradCAM works by computing gradients of the output with respect to intermediate feature maps, then weighting each feature channel by its average gradient magnitude. The resulting heatmap highlights regions where small changes would most affect the prediction, effectively showing where the network “pays attention” when making decisions. Originally developed for classification tasks, GradCAM can be adapted for regression by computing gradients with respect to the mean predicted value. For our analysis, we compute GradCAM heatmaps at multiple layers throughout the UNet and measure their correlation with two reference maps: (1) edge maps derived from ground truth depth via Sobel filtering, representing geometric boundaries; and (2) fringe intensity variation maps computed as the local standard deviation of fringe intensity, capturing where fringe patterns carry the most information. The logic of this comparison is straightforward: if the network learned physics-based fringe decoding, its attention should correlate with fringe patterns, the input signal that encodes depth information. Conversely, if the network relies on geometric shortcuts, its attention should correlate with edges, the boundaries that define object shapes but do not directly encode depth in the physics of FPP. sections.heading: 4.7.3 Flat Plane Out-of-Distribution Test
sections.text: The most direct way to test whether a network has learned a shortcut versus the intended solution is to present inputs where the shortcut fails but the correct solution should still work. This out-of-distribution (OOD) testing paradigm ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ) is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability: by carefully constructing test cases that dissociate the shortcut from the correct answer, we can definitively determine which strategy the network employs. For our hypothesis, the critical test case is an image containing valid fringe patterns but no geometric features , specifically a flat, featureless plane. If the network learned physics-based fringe decoding, it should correctly predict uniform depth corresponding to the plane’s distance; the fringe pattern encodes this depth regardless of whether edges are present. However, if the network relies on geometric shortcuts, it should fail catastrophically: with no edges to detect, the shape-based strategy has no basis for prediction. We captured a flat plane at 1.8 m, well within the trained depth range (Fig. 18 ). A physics-aware network should predict uniform depth across the plane corresponding to its distance from the projector. The key diagnostic is whether the network recognizes that a flat plane should produce flat depth. The results are striking. Instead of predicting a uniform depth that reflects the plane’s actual 1.8 m distance, the network predicts near-zero depth across most of the surface (mean = 0.088 normalized units), effectively classifying the flat plane itself as background. The prediction range extends to [ − - 1.19, 4.38], far outside the valid [0, 1] training range, with substantial portions of the image predicting physically impossible negative depth values. This behavior is consistent with a network that has learned to associate “no internal shape features” with “no object,” defaulting to background depth whenever the geometric shortcut has nothing to latch onto. GradCAM analysis (Fig. 19 ) provides additional context. Encoder layers (enc3, enc4) show strong activation across the fringes within the rectangular front plane, with comparatively little response to the fringes on the surrounding background. In contrast, the decoder layers (dec1, dec3, dec4) show minimal spatial attention. The network uses the rectangular boundary to define a region of interest and processes the fringe pattern selectively within it, yet still fails to convert that fringe information into a uniform depth estimate consistent with a flat surface. This is consistent with how the network processes images of complex objects (Table 8 ), where edge-correlated attention defines an object region and shape-based depth filling proceeds within it. With no learned internal shape template to fill in for a featureless plane, the network’s pipeline collapses to a near-zero (background) prediction even though encoder-stage attention is locally engaged with the fringe pattern. This failure mode directly confirms the shape prior hypothesis: the network implements a two-stage pipeline of (1) edge detection to identify object boundaries and define a region of interest, followed by (2) shape-based depth filling within that region. When presented with a flat surface lacking internal geometric structure, the network correctly detects the boundary and engages encoder attention with the fringes inside it, but the depth-filling stage has no learned shape template to map onto and the prediction collapses to background. The fringe pattern’s depth information is therefore reaching the encoder but not being translated into uniform depth, despite that information being present and physically sufficient.

sections.heading: 4.7.4 Implications for Single-Shot FPP
sections.text: These three analyses, linear probing, GradCAM attention mapping, and out-of-distribution testing, converge on a consistent mechanistic explanation: the UNet learns geometric shortcuts rather than fringe-to-depth physics. Each technique provides complementary evidence: • Linear probing demonstrates that geometric information (edges) is encoded 2.82 × \times more explicitly than depth values in the network’s internal representations, indicating the network prioritizes shape over physical quantities. • GradCAM reveals that during prediction, the network attends 1.28 × \times more strongly to geometric boundaries than to fringe intensity patterns, suggesting decisions are based on shape recognition rather than fringe analysis. • Flat plane testing shows that when presented with a flat surface lacking internal shape features, the encoder selectively attends to the fringes inside the bounded region but the network still collapses to a near-zero (background) prediction across the surface, indicating it cannot translate fringe information into uniform depth without a learned shape template to fill in. This mechanistic understanding explains why reconstruction error (14.54 mm, 18% of object depth range) remains high despite extensive architectural optimization: the network predicts depth by detecting object boundaries and filling with learned shape templates, not by extracting phase information from fringe patterns. The resulting predictions capture coarse object geometry but lack the fine-grained precision achievable through physics-based phase demodulation. Read against Section 4.2 , the diagnosis takes a sharper form: Proposition 1 shows that the mapping the network was asked to learn does not uniquely exist without fringe-order information, and the shortcut documented here is the specific way an optimizer trained on ℓ 1 \ell_{1} / ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regression resolves that non-injectivity (by collapsing onto whatever shape-prior surrogate the training distribution makes available). These findings have broader implications for the application of deep learning to optical metrology. Neural networks are powerful pattern recognizers, but they exploit whatever statistical regularities lead to low training loss, not necessarily the physical principles we intend them to learn. In our case, correlations between object shapes and their depth profiles provide an easier learning signal than the mathematically precise but spatially distributed fringe-to-depth relationship. Our results motivate hybrid approaches that explicitly incorporate physical constraints: either through physics-informed loss functions that penalize violations of fringe optics, network architectures that include differentiable phase extraction modules, or training procedures that encourage fringe pattern utilization. Simply providing more data or larger models is unlikely to overcome the fundamental tendency toward geometric shortcut learning demonstrated here.

sections.heading: 5 PhiCalNet: A Phase-Intermediate Architecture for Single-Shot FPP
sections.text: The mechanistic analysis in Section 4.7 showed that a depth-regressing UNet bypasses fringe physics and relies on object-shape priors, the same regime Section 4.2 identifies as ill-posed under single-shot acquisition. The closing of that section identifies the principled response: route the reconstruction through wrapped phase and fringe order rather than learning I t ↦ Z I_{t}\mapsto Z directly. To remove the shape-prior solution from the hypothesis space rather than merely discourage it via a loss penalty, we introduce PhiCalNet , a single-shot reconstruction architecture that realizes that recommended pipeline. Its operative design choice can be stated in one sentence: the network outputs a wrapped-phase representation ( sin ⁡ ϕ , cos ⁡ ϕ ) (\sin\phi,\cos\phi) rather than depth, and the only path from that output to the reconstructed depth runs through a fixed differentiable calibration layer that applies the FPP triangulation physics deterministically. Two architectural pieces are load-bearing. Phase representation : the network’s output space is wrapped phase, not depth, foreclosing the shape-prior solution because depth is never produced as a direct learned quantity. Fixed differentiable calibration : a non-learnable layer 𝒞 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{C}(\cdot) maps unwrapped phase to depth using the camera–projector geometry. The layer is differentiable, which makes depth-supervised loss terms definable on its output (used as one component of the composite training loss in Section 5.2 ) and activates a gradient path from the depth output back through the calibration into the learnable backbone that supports natural joint-learning extensions of the design (joint calibration learning, heteroscedastic depth likelihoods, multi-resolution depth losses, absolute-scale depth supervision; see Sections 5.2.1 and 6 ); its primary architectural role for the headline configuration, however, is to convert phase to depth deterministically in the forward pass. Neither piece is unprecedented in isolation: phase-intermediate networks with downstream calibration math have been used in FPP before ( Feng et al., 2019 ; Nguyen et al., 2019 ) , and depth-output networks are standard. Combining them, by making the network’s output space wrapped phase and inserting a fixed differentiable calibration layer that converts that output to depth, is the architectural choice that removes the shape-prior solution from the hypothesis space without a loss penalty. The only path from the network’s output to depth runs through 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and the only way to produce accurate depth at the output of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is for the network’s output to actually represent wrapped phase. The physics is therefore a hard architectural constraint, not a soft training signal. We describe the architecture in Section 5.1 , the training loss and a component-wise ablation in Section 5.2 , and report results and a residual-error analysis in Sections 5.3 – 5.5 . Section 5.4 runs the positive test of this design hypothesis: if the architectural framing is what is doing the work, then enforcing the same physics as a soft loss penalty on an otherwise unconstrained depth-regressing network (a PINN baseline) should not match PhiCalNet, because shape-prior solutions remain in the hypothesis space. Section 5.4 confirms exactly this.

sections.heading: 5.4 Positive Test of the Design Hypothesis: Loss-Level Physics Does Not Suffice
sections.text: The 3.3 × \times MAE improvement reported above follows from moving physics into the forward pass. The design hypothesis of Section 5 claims more sharply that this architectural framing is what is doing the work, and not merely the presence of calibration physics anywhere in the pipeline. The positive test of that hypothesis is the obvious alternative: keep depth as the network output but enforce the same physics as a soft loss penalty on the otherwise unconstrained depth-regressing network, which is the standard physics-informed neural network approach the machine learning literature would suggest by default. ( Raissi et al., 2019 ; Karniadakis et al., 2021 ) If the soft-penalty version closes the gap, the architectural framing is overdetermined; if it does not, the architectural choice is isolated as the operative factor. We refer to this alternative as PINN-UNet: the baseline UNet that predicts normalized depth D ^ norm \hat{D}_{\mathrm{norm}} , augmented with a differentiable inverse-calibration layer 𝒟 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{D}(\cdot) that maps predicted depth back to the phase that should have produced it, and trained with the objective ℒ PINN = ℒ HybridL1 + λ ⋅ ‖ 𝒟 ⁡ ( D ^ ) − Φ gt ‖ 1 , ℳ , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PINN}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HybridL1}}+\lambda\cdot\bigl\|\mathcal{D}(\hat{D})-\Phi_{\mathrm{gt}}\bigr\|_{1,\mathcal{M}}, (42) where ℒ HybridL1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HybridL1}} is the best-performing supervised loss from Section 4.5 and λ \lambda controls the strength of the physics term. The intent of Eq. ( 42 ) is that minimizing ℒ PINN \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PINN}} requires the network to produce depths that are both close to the ground truth and physically consistent with the observed fringe. Crucially, PINN-UNet and PhiCalNet are built on the same camera–projector calibration; only the point at which the physics is enforced (soft loss term vs. forward pass) differs. We trained four PINN-UNet variants at λ ∈ { 0.005 , 0.01 , 0.02 , 0.05 } \lambda\in\{0.005,0.01,\\ 0.02,0.05\} using the same data, optimizer, and schedule as the baseline UNet in Section 4.3 . The best variant ( λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 ) is statistically indistinguishable from the baseline (14.87 vs. 14.54 mm object MAE), and larger λ \lambda values degrade performance because the physics gradient competes with the supervised signal without constraining the representation. This pattern is consistent with a documented failure mode of physics-informed training. Krishnapriyan et al. ( Krishnapriyan et al., 2021 ) show that PINN losses do not, on their own, compel the network to learn the intended physical quantity when a lower-loss shortcut is available to the optimizer. Karniadakis et al. ( Karniadakis et al., 2021 ) and subsequent work ( Wang et al., 2024a ) have documented that the balance between supervised and physics terms is unstable and representation-dependent, and that the physics residual can be driven to low values by solutions that do not correspond to the target physics. In our setting the consequence is direct: as long as the network predicts depth, the physics penalty measures the residual of an already-learned depth field against a reconstruction that depends on it, and a shape-correct depth map produced through boundary detection can satisfy the physics term approximately without the network ever representing phase internally. The mechanistic result of Section 4.7 therefore persists even under a physics-informed loss. Moving physics into the architecture, as PhiCalNet does, is what forces phase to be used and produces the 3.3 × \times improvement reported in Table 10 .

sections.heading: 5.5.1 Oracle Outlier Exclusion
sections.text: To quantify how concentrated the error tail is, we evaluate an oracle-exclusion bound on the same predictions. For each threshold T ∈ { 100,200,500 } T\in\{100,200,500\} mm we remove pixels with absolute error exceeding T T and recompute MAE and RMSE over the remaining pixels. This is an upper bound on any post-hoc correction scheme: a real method must identify the bad pixels without access to ground truth, and the oracle identifies them exactly. Table 13 : Oracle-exclusion analysis on PhiCalNet predictions. Pixels with absolute error greater than the threshold are removed from the test object mask before MAE and RMSE are recomputed. The ceiling shows what any post-hoc outlier rejector could achieve at best. Object-level MAE and RMSE reported in millimeters. Condition Pixels Removed % of Mask MAE RMSE No removal 0 0.000% 4.07 20.28 Exclude err > > 500 mm 1,059 0.053% 3.64 7.54 Exclude err > > 200 mm 1,221 0.061% 3.62 7.04 Exclude err > > 100 mm 2,060 0.103% 3.57 6.46 Removing 0.103% of the object mask reduces RMSE from 20.28 mm to 6.46 mm, a 3.1 × \times reduction, while MAE moves only from 4.07 to 3.57 mm (Table 13 ). This ceiling is informative in two ways. First, PhiCalNet is near-oracle on 99.9% of pixels. Second, the remaining RMSE gap is not a fitting error that additional loss engineering is likely to close. The ground-truth wrapped phase is a discontinuous function at every ± π \pm\pi crossing; no continuous regressor can track it exactly there, and whenever the network’s ( s ^ , c ^ ) (\hat{s},\hat{c}) straddles the wrap, the resulting atan2 \mathrm{atan2} output lies on the wrong side. The magnitude of that mistake is independent of how close the prediction is: even a vanishingly small sign error produces a full 2 ​ π 2\pi displacement in ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} , and therefore a full fringe period of depth error. Classical spatial phase-unwrapping algorithms encounter a structurally similar failure in the same regime. ( Goldstein et al., 1988 ; Zuo et al., 2016 ) Multi-frame phase shifting resolves the ambiguity by construction because the additional frames reconstruct ϕ gt \phi_{\mathrm{gt}} analytically per pixel, removing the need for a continuous regressor to approximate a discontinuous target. The 3 × \times object-MAE gap between single-shot and multi-shot reconstruction observed throughout this paper therefore reflects an information-theoretic deficit of single-frame acquisition rather than a modeling limitation of the learner.

sections.heading: 5.6 Multi-Frame Extension and Fringe-Order Sensitivity
sections.text: The preceding error analysis argues on theoretical grounds that the single-shot residual is information-limited and that the oracle- k k assumption is physically necessary rather than convenient. We now validate both claims empirically. Three experiments are reported: (i) a multi-frame extension of PhiCalNet to verify that more observational information closes the wrap-boundary gap, (ii) a learned- k k ablation that removes the oracle assumption and observes how the pipeline degrades, and (iii) a fringe-order sensitivity sweep that quantifies how much upstream k k noise the pipeline can absorb without degrading depth accuracy.

All other factors (loss formulation, optimizer, oracle- k k assumption) are held fixed. Table 14 reports the result alongside the existing single-shot baseline. The network absorbs the easy geometry via shape priors, the same pathology identified mechanistically in Section 4.7 , and fails on geometries where shape priors do not disambiguate fringe order. Counter-intuitively, the capacity-rich fully-learned Variant L at 3 frames outperforms the capacity-sparse hybrid Variant H at 3 frames (596 vs. 1439 mm MAE) despite the hybrid receiving physics-exact wrapped phase as input. The widened head is a better memorizer of training-distribution geometries but a worse generalizer to test-distribution geometries, extending the per-sample class-specific failure signature visible in both Variant L and Variant H. These three variants, spanning three orders of magnitude of k k -head capacity (0.4 M / 4 M / 3.3 M dedicated to k k , or 0.4 M / 31.4 M / 34.3 M including the phase backbone), all fail in the same structured way: near-perfect performance on smooth geometries where shape priors disambiguate the fringe order, and catastrophic failure on complex multi-level geometries where they do not. Additional capacity moves the model further into the memorization regime rather than toward a successful general k k -predictor. We therefore conclude that k k -prediction from a small number of fringe frames is an ill-posed problem under the information content available, rather than an under-trained or under-parameterized one.

sections.heading: 5.7 Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
sections.text: Section 4.7 applied linear probing, GradCAM attention mapping, and out-of-distribution flat-plane testing to the UNet baseline and concluded that the network learns a geometric shortcut: shape templates are encoded more explicitly than depth values, attention concentrates on object boundaries rather than fringe patterns, and the network fails on a featureless plane that retains valid fringes. The error analysis of Section 5.5 attributed PhiCalNet’s residual error to wrap-boundary sign flips in the predicted wrapped phase, a localized failure mode that is mechanistically different from the diffuse shape-prior failure of the UNet baseline. The natural question is whether the same three interpretability techniques, applied to PhiCalNet, support that mechanistic distinction directly: does PhiCalNet represent and attend to the fringe-to-phase relationship its architecture prescribes, or has the phase-intermediate framing been bypassed by another shortcut the calibration layer happens to permit? We therefore apply the same battery of techniques to PhiCalNet, with two adaptations needed for the phase-intermediate architecture. First, the probing target set is extended from { \{ edges, depth } \} to { \{ edges, depth, sin ⁡ ϕ \sin\phi , cos ϕ } \cos\phi\} , because phase, not depth, is the network’s trained output and the asymmetry between phase decoding and depth decoding is itself diagnostic. Second, GradCAM is computed in two modes: phase mode , in which gradients are taken with respect to the mean of the network’s ( s ^ , c ^ ) (\hat{s},\hat{c}) output, and depth mode , in which gradients flow through the (analytical) unwrap and calibration steps to the final depth prediction. The phase mode answers “what does the network attend to when computing its trained output?” and the depth mode answers “what does it attend to when we backpropagate from the deployment output?”. The contrast between the two modes, on the same trained weights, is informative about whether the network’s competence really resides at the phase stage.
